messages.subject: testNbElites
parts:
Hi there,

I wonder about the semantics of "testing" right now.

In my setup, I use

testNbElites = 10
testIterationElites = 1

and the irace run with 1000 experiments end up having a few iterations. In the end, testing is done on 5 configurations (not on a number that is closer to 5*10). Each of the iterations returns the same "Best configuration", so the following question: which instances are tested in my case? :) Below is an example.

Thank you!

ps: iteration count bug? see below: "Iteration 4 of 5", "Iteration 6 of 6", ...

Cheers,
Markus

--

messages.subject: Re: [irace-package] testNbElites
parts: Hi Markus,

On 15/05/17 10:18, M. Wagner wrote:
> I wonder about the semantics of "testing" right now.
>
> In my setup, I use
>
> testNbElites = 10
> testIterationElites = 1
>
> and the irace run with 1000 experiments end up having a few iterations. In the
> end, testing is done on 5 configurations (not on a number that is closer to
> 5*10). Each of the iterations returns the same "Best configuration", so the
> following question: which instances are tested in my case? :) Below is an example.

The way this works is explained in Sect 7. If you can point out what part is
not clear, perhaps I can re-write it in a clearer way.

In a nutshell, testIterationElites controls whether only the final elites or
also the elites at each iteration are tested. The elites are those
configurations that are still alive at the end of a race, which can be even
just one. testNbElites is a maximum in the number of elites tested from each
iteration, the actual number of elites at any particular iteration may be
smaller. Finally, we only test each configuration once. That is, if an elite
appears in iteration 2 and survives until the end, it is only tested once. By
"testing", we mean that a configuration is evaluated on all test instances as
provided by testInstancesDir/testInstancesFile.
> ps: iteration count bug? see below: "Iteration 4 of 5", "Iteration 6 of 6", ...

There is an "Iteration 5 of 5" between those two. Iterated F-race estimates a
minimum number of iterations to perform, however, depending on what happens
while running, there may enough budget left to keep running, thus irace adjusts
itself to keep going on. The iteration number also controls how exploratory the
sampling is, thus sometimes irace may skip iterations because one particular
iteration is not feasible with the remaining budget. This is all explained and
specified in the ORP paper.

Cheers,

Manuel.

On 16/05/17 13:35, M. Wagner wrote:
> Since you state “can be further sorted according to their mean value” —>
> this is happening now, right? I am just a little curious when the word “can”
> is used.

This happens already when we print out the elites at the end of each
iteration/race and at the end before testing (Best configurations).

> Since you state “mean value or sum of ranks” —> which one is it, or how
> would I know which criteria is used? Just curious…

This depends on the testType (--test-type). If you use the F-test (the
default), they are sorted according to their sum of ranks (which is the same as
mean rank in this context) If you use the t-test, they are sorted according to
the mean value.

> The reason I keep asking: I had another irace run where the “tested
> configurations” ended up being sorted (almost perfectly) the wrong way
> around. Yes, I know there is a big random component in my setup. My testing
> used 1 million repetitions (!) then (in the testing only!) and the “further
> down ones” in the list of “tested configurations” ended up being better than
> the “further up ones” (note that I am avoiding the words “top”/“worst”
> here). Yes, due to randomness… still, it was worth asking whether there is
> an underlying system behind the way the configurations are listed (yes,
> based on the experiments, the races, the randomness, and then sorting). Ok.

The system is as follows (and I'm going to update the output of irace to make
this obvious, thanks for pointing it out):

* Elite configurations and the final "# Best configurations" are sorted from
best to worst (on the subset of the training set that they have been evaluated
on) according to sum of ranks (F-test) or mean value (t-test).

* Other printouts of configurations are either in the order in which they were
generated or with an arbitrary order.

Thus, the configurations to be tested (the list after "# Testing
configurations:") may be in an arbitrary order. Actually, I'm not sure we can
print any sensible order when mixing iteration-elites from different
iterations, since an elite that was discarded in iteration 3 will have results
on different training instances than an elite that was discarded in iteration
6. Note that we print these configurations to be tested before evaluating them
on the test instances. We don't try to sort them after testing and the final "#
Testing results" matrix is not sorted according to performance. Perhaps it
would be useful to sort it? On the other hand, one should not do any further
tuning or selection based on the test results; otherwise you are doing tuning
on the test instances, which betrays the reason for separating training and
testing instances. It will be methodologically wrong to select the best
configuration among the elites according to the results on the test instances.

Ideally, if you compare the testing results of the elites that survived until
the end to testing results of the elites that were discarded before reaching
the end, the former should have a higher performance. There are many reasons
this may not be true (the latter were not evaluated on as many instances as the
former and the additional instances are quite different from the common ones,
the train instances may actually not be correlated with the test instances,
randomness/unlucky runs may have killed early the best configurations), but it
tends to be rare that this happens outside artificial setups.

If you send me the irace.Rdata file privately, it will be easy to check what
went wrong.

Perhaps we can print a final report on average performance on training vs
testing for all elites tested at the end.

Cheers,

Manuel.

parts:
On 18/05/17 01:57, M. Wagner wrote:
> A very good point! I was very tempted to support the sorting, however, I agree
> with you. Better don’t sort it. Some people might have very good reasons to
> pick the best from the training set (I have some right now ;), but it is better
> to leave them either in the current semi-unsorted order.

Just to be completely clear. It is OK to pick the best from the *training* set
results. Those are the configurations printed after the line:

# Best configurations (first number is the configuration ID; sorted from best
to worst according to the sum of ranks)

and they are sorted from best (on the training set) to worst (note the new text
explaining the sorting).

What is not OK is to pick the best by looking at the *test* set results. They
are there just to let you know what happens for "unseen" instances not tuned for.

It is like doing 30 runs to calculate mean performance, but then re-running
those runs that are pretty bad. Yes, one would get better results but also fool
one-self about what is the actual mean performance.

Actually, the ideal way would be to do what ML people do: have three sets,
training, validation and test, then do cross-validation with various tuning
runs and pick the best configuration according to the validation set, then
compare with other algorithms on the test set (but not do more selection or
tuning). However, this will be extremely expensive in most real-world scenarios
and probably hard to explain to typical reviewers. First let's get to the point
where almost everybody accepts the training/test separation and automatic
configuration as a default step in algorithm design and analysis :)

Cheers,

Manuel.
